fields.before:
In a perspective picture on a flat plane, a sphere is drawn as a circle only when it lies on the central axis. Elsewhere its outline is an ellipse whose long axis points at the principal point. For a sphere that subtends the half-angle $\alpha$ and lies at the angle $\theta$ off the axis, the ratio of the axes is
$$\frac{\cos\alpha}{\sqrt{\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\alpha}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\cos\theta}.$$
The stretching grows without bound toward $90^\circ$, so wide-angle pictures smear spheres, faces and columns near their edges. From the exact station point the ellipses look round again, but at ordinary viewing distances they look wrong, and painters have often drawn off-axis spheres as circles anyway; the globes held by Ptolemy and Zoroaster in Raphael’s *School of Athens* are the classic case.
fields.after:
Assume the eye is outside the sphere and its entire tangent cone lies in front of the eye: its angular radius and off-axis angle satisfy $0<\alpha$, $0\le\theta$ and $\theta+\alpha<90^\circ$. In a perspective picture on a flat plane, this sphere is drawn as a circle only on the central axis. Elsewhere its outline is a finite ellipse whose long axis points at the principal point. For a sphere that subtends the half-angle $\alpha$ and lies at the angle $\theta$ off the axis, the ratio of the axes is
$$\frac{\cos\alpha}{\sqrt{\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\alpha}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\cos\theta}.$$
For fixed $\alpha$, the stretching grows without bound as $\theta$ approaches $90^\circ-\alpha$ from below; $1/\cos\theta$ is a small-angular-radius approximation away from this boundary. Wide-angle pictures therefore stretch off-axis spheres near their edges. From the exact station point the ellipses look round again, but at ordinary viewing distances they look wrong, and painters have often drawn off-axis spheres as circles anyway; the globes held by Ptolemy and Zoroaster in Raphael’s *School of Athens* are the classic case.

fields.before:
The rays from the eye that graze a sphere form a circular cone around the line of sight to its centre (art-1.1), and the picture of the sphere is the section of that cone by the picture plane (art-1.2). For a sphere straight ahead the plane cuts the cone at right angles and the section is a circle; for a sphere at angle $\theta$ the cut is oblique, and an oblique section of a circular cone is an ellipse, stretched about $1/\cos\theta$ times along the radial direction. The cross-section on the right shows the chord on the picture line growing toward the margin even though every sphere subtends the same angle. The retina, curved around the eye, receives every sphere as a round patch, which is why the ellipses look wrong (art-1.10).

The axis calculation is a quadratic-form calculation (ladr 9.23). Rotate picture coordinates so the centre direction is (sinθ,cosθ,0), with rays q=(x,d,z). Tangency gives (q·n)²=cos²α |q|². Its quadratic coefficients in the radial and transverse directions are A=cos²θ−sin²α and cos²α. When A>0, translation completes the square; the squared semiaxes are d²sin²α cos²α/A² and d²sin²α/A. Their ratio is the stated cosα/√A. Positive definiteness is essential: the algebra does not classify every oblique cone cut as a bounded ellipse.
fields.after:

fields.before:
Let four points $A,B,C,D$ lie on a line, at signed positions $a,b,c,d$ along it. Their **cross-ratio**
$$(A,B;C,D)=\frac{(c-a)(d-b)}{(c-b)(d-a)}$$
is unchanged by central projection: if the four points are projected from any centre $O$ onto any other line, the images $A',B',C',D'$ have the same cross-ratio. Lengths, ratios of lengths and midpoints are not preserved; the cross-ratio is the simplest quantity that is. In particular, four equally spaced points (fence posts, columns) have cross-ratio $4/3$ in every perspective picture.
fields.after:
Let four distinct points $A,B,C,D$ lie on a line, at signed positions $a,b,c,d$ along it. Their **cross-ratio**
$$(A,B;C,D)=\frac{(c-a)(d-b)}{(c-b)(d-a)}$$
is unchanged by central projection: if the four points are projected from a centre $O$ off their line onto another coplanar line, with four finite distinct images, the images $A',B',C',D'$ have the same cross-ratio. Lengths, ratios of lengths and midpoints are not preserved; the cross-ratio is the simplest quantity that is. In particular, four equally spaced points (fence posts, columns) have cross-ratio $4/3$ in every perspective picture.

fields.before: In “projection”, drag the four points along the bottom line, the centre $O$, and the ends of the two other lines: distances and their ratios change from line to line, the cross-ratio does not. In “colonnade”, equally spaced columns are pictured at uneven spacings, but any four in a row have cross-ratio $4/3$, which predicts where the next column must stand; drag the vanishing point and the first column.
fields.after: In “projection”, drag the four points along the bottom line, the centre $O$, and the ends of the two other lines: distances and their ratios change from line to line, the cross-ratio does not. In “colonnade”, equally spaced columns are pictured at uneven spacings, but any four consecutive columns have cross-ratio $4/3$, which predicts where the next column must stand; drag the vanishing point and the first column.

fields.before:
Choose an eye point $E$ and a canvas plane $\Pi$. To paint an object so that it looks undistorted from $E$, imagine it drawn normally on a picture plane $\Pi'$ perpendicular to the line of sight from $E$, and then **project it from $E$ onto $\Pi$**: each point $P$ of the intended picture is painted where the line $EP$ crosses the canvas.

Seen from $E$, the painted canvas and the intended picture send the eye the same rays, so they look identical. Seen from anywhere else, the painting is a smear: if the line of sight meets the canvas at the angle $\varphi$, the image is stretched across the canvas by the factor $1/\sin\varphi$, which is large for a grazing point of view.
fields.after:
Choose an eye point $E$ and a canvas plane $\Pi$. To paint an object so that it looks undistorted from $E$, imagine it drawn normally on a picture plane $\Pi'$ perpendicular to the central line of sight from $E$ and through its intersection with $\Pi$, and then **project it from $E$ onto $\Pi$**: each point $P$ of the intended picture is painted where the line $EP$ crosses the canvas.

Seen from $E$, the painted canvas and the intended picture send the eye the same rays, so they look identical. Seen from anywhere else, the painting is a smear: if the line of sight meets the canvas at the angle $\varphi$, the central local scale along the tilt is $1/\sin\varphi$, which is large for a grazing point of view. This is a differential scale at that central intersection; a finite image undergoes a projective warp with position-dependent scale.

fields.before: This is central projection (art-1.2) used backwards. A perspective picture is the cross-section of the visual pyramid with the canvas; the intended picture and its shadow on the canvas are two cross-sections of the same pyramid, so from the apex they cover each other exactly. Tilting the canvas relative to the plane perpendicular to the sight line stretches distances along the tilt by $1/\sin\varphi$ and leaves the perpendicular direction alone, which is why Holbein's skull is a long sliver along the floor of the picture.
fields.after: This is central projection (art-1.2) used backwards. A perspective picture is the cross-section of the visual pyramid with the canvas; the intended picture and its shadow on the canvas are two cross-sections of the same pyramid, so from the apex they cover each other exactly. At the central intersection of the two picture planes, the derivative of this projection has scale $1/\sin\varphi$ along the tilt and scale one in the perpendicular direction. Away from that point its scale changes with position; the finite projection is not a uniform stretch. This explains the long anamorphic image without replacing the computed projective map by an affine one.

fields.before:
Whatever the answer, the logic is a statistical one. The test is: fit the best single projective camera (a $3\times4$ matrix with 11 parameters) to the known 3D shape and its painted image, and look at the leftover misfit. A traced image has small misfit; but so does an image constructed with care, and a bigger misfit does not exclude tracing in pieces from several lens positions. The decisive quantity is therefore the unaided accuracy of the painters of the time, which is exactly what is in dispute. The experiment below is synthetic: a made-up chandelier and your own assumed error sizes, not measurements of any painting.

The actual camera fit is homogeneous DLT: the normalized point equations form a real matrix A and a unit camera vector p is chosen to minimize |Ap|². The real spectral theorem ladr 7.29 diagonalizes the symmetric matrix AᵀA in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Writing p in that basis makes pᵀAᵀAp a weighted average of its eigenvalues, so a smallest-eigenvalue eigenvector minimizes this algebraic residual. The subsequently reported reprojection RMS is a different quantity; this fit is not a guarantee of its global minimum or a historical test identifying tracing.

fields.before:
The black-body spectrum depends on one parameter, $T$ (art-3.10), so its chromaticities form a curve (art-4.7); a general white light is described by two numbers, and CCT is the projection onto that curve. The projection is done in $(u,v)$ because that plane is more perceptually uniform than $(x,y)$ (a rough forerunner of art-5.5): the nearest point there is the black body that looks most like the light. McCamy’s cubic in $n=(x-0.3320)/(y-0.1858)$ is a quick empirical approximation of the same number near daylight.

The normal-line construction uses the interior-extremum criterion pma 5.8. For a differentiable locus r(T) in the declared uv plane and a fixed test point q, differentiate squared distance: D′(T)=2(r(T)−q)·r′(T). A differentiable interior closest point must have D′=0, hence its displacement is perpendicular to a nonzero tangent. This is a necessary local condition, not a uniqueness guarantee, and finite table endpoints require separate checks. The widget searches its sampled locus; its finite nearest-point result is not an exact continuum or perceptual certificate.

fields.before:
For a pinhole of diameter $d$ at distance $f$ in front of the screen, the image of a distant point has two competing widths. The **geometric blur**, the shadow of the hole, is $b_g\approx d$ and shrinks with the hole. The **diffraction blur**, the Airy pattern of a circular aperture, has width $b_d\approx 2.44\,\lambda f/d$ and grows as the hole shrinks. The total is smallest when the two are comparable,
$$d_{\rm opt}\approx\sqrt{2.44\,\lambda f},\qquad b_{\min}\approx\sqrt2\,d_{\rm opt},$$
with the factor depending on how the blurs are combined and measured (Rayleigh's own optimum has a slightly different constant). No pinhole gives a sharper picture than this, which is why photographic pinholes are about $0.2$–$0.4$ mm wide.
fields.after:
For a pinhole of diameter $d$ at distance $f$ in front of the screen, the image of a distant point has two competing widths. The **geometric blur**, the shadow of the hole, is $b_g\approx d$ and shrinks with the hole. The **diffraction blur**, the Airy pattern of a circular aperture, has width $b_d\approx 2.44\,\lambda f/d$ and grows as the hole shrinks. For the root-sum-square proxy $b(d)=\sqrt{d^2+(2.44\lambda f/d)^2}$, the total is smallest when these two widths are equal,
$$d_{\rm opt}\approx\sqrt{2.44\,\lambda f},\qquad b_{\min}\approx\sqrt2\,d_{\rm opt},$$
with the factor depending on how the blurs are combined and measured (Rayleigh's own optimum has a slightly different constant). This proxy minimum is not a universal exact diffraction bound. The computed 84%-energy Fresnel diameter below uses a different, explicit numerical criterion; its sampled minimum can differ from this estimate.

fields.before: Geometry (art-2.3) says the blur grows linearly in $d$. Wave optics says a circular aperture of diameter $d$ cannot send light into an angle smaller than about $1.22\,\lambda/d$, so at distance $f$ the spot has diameter $2.44\,\lambda f/d$, falling as $1/d$. A decreasing and an increasing function of $d$ have a minimum where they cross. The picture below does not use these two formulas to draw the spot: it integrates the Fresnel diffraction integral of the circular hole, so the blur is the true one in between the two regimes too.
fields.after: Geometry (art-2.3) says the blur grows linearly in $d$. Wave optics says a circular aperture of diameter $d$ cannot send light into an angle smaller than about $1.22\,\lambda/d$, so at distance $f$ the spot has diameter $2.44\,\lambda f/d$, falling as $1/d$. For the declared root-sum-square proxy, squaring gives $b^2=d^2+k^2/d^2$ with $k=2.44\lambda f$. Its derivative vanishes at $d^4=k^2$, giving equal terms and the stated minimum. Arbitrary increasing and decreasing functions do not imply that rule. The picture below does not use these two formulas to draw the spot: it integrates the Fresnel diffraction integral of the circular hole, giving a numerical Fresnel-model estimate between the regimes. Finite radial quadrature, the approximate Bessel function and the sampled diameter search do not certify an exact continuum minimum.

fields.before: Slide the pinhole diameter $d$ across the valley of the curve (left, logarithmic axes): the exact spot size, from the Fresnel integral, follows the two asymptotes and bottoms out near $d_{\rm opt}$. On the right, two point sources are imaged; at small $d$ the Airy rings appear, at large $d$ the two geometric discs overlap. Change the screen distance $f$, the wavelength, and the separation of the two sources.
